CWE-362.name: Concurrent Execution using Shared Resource with Improper Synchronization ('Race Condition')
CWE-362.question: Does this function access shared data or a resource that another thread or process can change, with a window where it is not protected by proper synchronisation?

any: a global, static or shared variable is read, tested and then written without holding a lock across the whole sequence
a check on a shared value or file is followed by an action that relies on the check, with no lock or atomic operation joining them
some accesses to a shared variable hold a lock and others in this function do not
the shared accesses happen while holding the same lock, or use atomic operations for the whole read-modify-write
the data is local, thread-local or immutable after initialisation
the code is single-threaded and installs no signal handlers

distinguish_from.CWE-367: the race is between checking a file or resource and then using it
distinguish_from.CWE-366: the race is between threads over a shared variable within one process
distinguish_from.CWE-364: the race involves a signal handler

CWE-363.name: Race Condition Enabling Link Following
CWE-363.question: Does this function check a file or directory's status and then open or modify it by path, leaving a gap in which it could be swapped for a link?

any: a path is checked for existence, type, owner or permissions and later opened, written, chmod-ed or deleted by the same path name
c: stat, lstat or access on a path followed by open, fopen, chown, chmod or unlink on that same path
cpp: std::filesystem::exists, is_regular_file, is_symlink or status on a path, then std::ofstream, permissions or remove on the same path
python: os.path.exists, os.path.islink, os.stat or os.access followed by open, os.chmod or shutil calls on the path
javascript: fs.existsSync, fs.statSync or fs.access followed by fs.open, fs.writeFile or fs.chmod on the path
rust: Path::exists, symlink_metadata or metadata followed by File::open or fs::write on the path

any: the file is opened first and checks are made on the open descriptor, such as fstat
the open uses flags that refuse links or require a new file, such as O_NOFOLLOW or O_CREAT with O_EXCL
the directory involved is private to the process and not writable by others

distinguish_from.CWE-367: the check and use concern something other than a file that could be replaced with a link

CWE-364.name: Signal Handler Race Condition
CWE-364.question: Is this function a signal handler, or does it install one, in a way that lets the handler race with normal code or with itself over shared state?

c: a function registered with signal or sigaction modifies global data that the main code also changes, without blocking the signal
a handler frees memory, closes files or changes data structures that other code may be using when the signal arrives
a handler calls longjmp or exit while the interrupted code may be part-way through an update
a handler that calls signal() to re-install itself, which races where the handler is reset on delivery
cpp: a signal handler changes a std::vector, std::string or other object, or locks a std::mutex, that normal code also uses

c: the handler only sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag that the main loop polls
signals are blocked with sigprocmask or sa_mask around the shared-state updates
the function neither defines nor installs a signal handler
cpp: the handler only stores to a lock-free std::atomic or a volatile std::sig_atomic_t flag

distinguish_from.CWE-479: the handler calls a non-reentrant library function
distinguish_from.CWE-831: the same handler is registered for several signals

CWE-366.name: Race Condition within a Thread
CWE-366.question: Can two threads run this function's code on the same shared variable or object at once, with a read-modify-write or multi-step update that is not protected by a lock or atomic operation?

c: a global, static or heap object reachable from several threads is updated with ++, +=, or read-then-write, without holding a mutex
a shared pointer is tested and then freed, replaced or initialised without a lock (for example lazy initialisation without once-semantics)
a thread routine passed to pthread_create or std::thread modifies data the creating code also uses
different threads write adjacent bit-fields of one struct, which share a memory location, without a common lock
cpp: a std::atomic updated with x = x + 1, x = !x or x = x * 2, which is a separate load and store rather than one atomic operation

c: every access to the shared data happens while holding the same mutex
the update uses atomic types or atomic intrinsics covering the whole operation
the data is local or thread-local, or only read after being fully initialised before threads start
cpp: initialisation uses std::call_once or a function-local static
fetch_add, fetch_xor, compare_exchange or a lock makes the update a single atomic step

distinguish_from.CWE-367: the race is between checking and using a file or external resource
distinguish_from.CWE-364: the competing code is a signal handler rather than another thread

CWE-367.name: Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) Race Condition
CWE-367.question: Does this function check the state of a file or other shared resource and then act on it in a separate step, so the state can change in between?

any: a file path is checked (exists, access, stat, permissions, is-symlink) and the same path is then opened, created, deleted or changed by a separate call
c: access() or stat() is followed by open() or fopen() on the same path
cpp: std::filesystem::exists or status on a path, then std::ifstream, std::ofstream or std::filesystem::rename on that path
python: os.path.exists, os.access or os.path.isfile is followed by open, os.remove or os.rename on the same path
javascript: fs.existsSync or fs.access is followed by fs.open, fs.writeFile or fs.unlink on the same path
rust: Path::exists or fs::metadata is followed by File::create, fs::write or fs::remove_file on the same path

any: the operation is done in one atomic call and its error is handled, such as open with O_CREAT|O_EXCL, or create_new(true)
the check is made on an already-open handle (fstat on the descriptor) rather than the path
the resource is private to the process, such as a local variable or an in-memory structure behind a lock held across check and use

distinguish_from.CWE-362: the race is between threads on shared memory rather than a check followed by a use of an external resource

CWE-368.name: Context Switching Race Condition
CWE-368.question: Does this function switch between security contexts (user, privilege level, origin or document) in several non-atomic steps, leaving a window where actions run in the wrong context?

any: privileges, credentials or the current user are changed in separate steps with work done between them
a navigation, document or origin change updates the security context after new content or callbacks may already run
the effective identity is lowered or raised for an operation and an error path skips restoring it
c: seteuid, setegid or setgroups called in sequence with calls between them that act on files or input

any: the context switch is done by a single atomic call or completed before any other work happens
callbacks and untrusted content are blocked until the new context is fully in place
the function does not change security context

distinguish_from.CWE-362: the race is over shared data rather than a security context switch

CWE-412.name: Unrestricted Externally Accessible Lock
CWE-412.question: Does this function rely on a lock that outside actors can create, hold or remove, such as a lock file in a shared directory or a lock keyed by user input?

any: a lock file is created or checked in a world-writable directory such as /tmp using a predictable name
a lock name, key or id comes from user input, letting a caller take or hold the lock
a lock can be held indefinitely by a client with no timeout or ownership check
the lock lives in a private location or in process memory unreachable from outside
the lock has a timeout or ownership check so one actor cannot hold it forever
the function does not use locks

distinguish_from.CWE-414: the code skips checking the lock rather than using one outsiders control

CWE-413.name: Improper Resource Locking
CWE-413.question: Does this function operate on a shared resource that needs exclusive access (file, record, shared memory, global) without locking it for the whole operation?

any: a shared file is read, modified and rewritten with no file lock or atomic replace
a shared record is read and updated in separate statements with no transaction, row lock or version check
shared memory or a global is modified while other code may access it, with no lock held
a lock, transaction or atomic operation covers the whole read-modify-write
the resource is private to this thread or process

distinguish_from.CWE-362: the race is a general unsynchronised access rather than a missing lock on an exclusive resource
distinguish_from.CWE-591: the missing lock is a memory page lock for sensitive data

CWE-414.name: Missing Lock Check
CWE-414.question: Does this function perform a sensitive operation on a resource that is protected by a lock without first checking or acquiring that lock?

any: other code guards the resource with a lock, flag or lock file, but this function modifies it without checking or taking the lock
a lock-held flag or try-lock result is obtained and then ignored before the operation proceeds
the function acquires the lock or verifies it is held before the operation
the function's contract states the caller already holds the lock, shown for example by an assertion
the resource is not shared or not protected by any lock

distinguish_from.CWE-413: no lock exists for the resource at all
distinguish_from.CWE-412: the lock exists but outside actors can control it

CWE-432.name: Dangerous Signal Handler not Disabled During Sensitive Operations
CWE-432.question: Does this signal handler update state shared with other handlers without blocking those other signals while it runs?

any: two or more signal handlers modify the same global or shared variables and none masks the others
c: sigaction is used with an empty sa_mask, or signal() is used, for handlers sharing state
python: several signal.signal handlers update the same module-level state with no signal.pthread_sigmask around the update
javascript: several process.on signal handlers mutate shared state while an async update may be in progress
rust: signal-hook or libc handlers for different signals modify the same static data

any: each handler only sets its own atomic flag
other signals are masked while the handler runs, for example via sa_mask
no state is shared between the handlers

distinguish_from.CWE-831: one handler function is registered for several signals
distinguish_from.CWE-828: the handler calls code that is not async-signal-safe

CWE-479.name: Signal Handler Use of a Non-reentrant Function
CWE-479.question: Does this signal handler call a non-reentrant library function such as malloc, free, printf, strtok or syslog?

c: a function registered with signal or sigaction calls malloc, free, realloc, printf, fprintf, syslog, strtok, localtime or exit
a handler calls a helper that itself uses stdio or the heap
cpp: a signal handler uses std::cout, new or delete, throws, or locks a std::mutex

c: the handler calls only async-signal-safe functions such as write, _exit or signal
the handler only sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag
the function is not used as a signal handler
cpp: the handler only stores to a lock-free std::atomic or a volatile std::sig_atomic_t flag

distinguish_from.CWE-828: the handler's unsafe work is changing shared structures rather than calling a non-reentrant function
distinguish_from.REL-168: the code merely uses signal.h signal handling at all

CWE-543.name: Use of Singleton Pattern Without Synchronization in a Multithreaded Context
CWE-543.question: Does this C++ function lazily create or return a singleton instance in multithreaded code without making the creation thread-safe?

any: a getInstance-style function tests a static pointer for null and then allocates the instance with new, with no mutex, std::call_once or atomic around the test and assignment
the singleton check uses a plain (non-atomic) pointer in double-checked form, testing it outside the lock
the instance is a function-local static (Meyers singleton), whose initialisation is thread-safe since C++11
creation is wrapped in std::call_once, a held std::mutex, or an atomic with correct ordering
the instance is created eagerly before any threads start

distinguish_from.CWE-609: the code uses a lock with a double-checked test and the flaw is the unsafe outer check

CWE-558.name: Use of getlogin() in Multithreaded Application
CWE-558.question: Does this function call getlogin() in a program that runs multiple threads?

c: getlogin() is called and its result used, in code reachable from more than one thread
getlogin() is used to decide on privileges or identity
getlogin_r is used with a caller buffer
the user identity is taken from getuid or geteuid with getpwuid_r
the function does not call getlogin

distinguish_from.CWE-663: a different non-reentrant function is called concurrently

CWE-591.name: Sensitive Data Storage in Improperly Locked Memory
CWE-591.question: Does this function hold secrets such as keys or passwords in memory that is not locked against being swapped to disk?

c: a buffer for a key, password or private data is allocated with malloc or on the stack with no mlock or VirtualLock
mlock or VirtualLock is called but its return value is ignored
rust: secret material held in an ordinary Vec or String with no memory locking or secrets crate
any: long-lived secret material is kept in ordinary memory with no attempt to prevent paging

c: the secret buffer is locked with mlock or VirtualLock and the result is checked
any: the data handled is not sensitive
python: Python and JavaScript offer no page locking for ordinary objects; report only if the code calls a locking API and ignores failure
javascript: JavaScript offers no page locking for ordinary objects; report only if the code calls a locking API and ignores failure

distinguish_from.CWE-226: the secret is not wiped before memory is freed or reused

CWE-662.name: Improper Synchronization
CWE-662.question: Does the function touch data, files or resources that other threads, processes, signal handlers or async tasks may use at the same time?

any: global, static or shared variables are read and written, with or without locks
threads, tasks or processes are started, or locks, mutexes, semaphores or atomics are used
a signal handler is installed or defined, or a non-reentrant function is called
a file or resource is checked and then used, where another actor could change it in between
the function works only on local variables and its arguments, with no shared state, threads, locks or signals
the function is pure computation with no I/O

CWE-663.name: Use of a Non-reentrant Function in a Concurrent Context
CWE-663.question: Does this function call a non-reentrant function (one using internal static state) from code that can run concurrently in several threads or a signal handler?

c: strtok, localtime, gmtime, asctime, ctime, rand, getenv-and-modify, readdir or gethostbyname used in thread or handler code
a helper with function-local static buffers is called from several threads
cpp: std::strtok, std::localtime, std::rand or a function-local static that is modified after initialisation, reached from std::thread code
python: a function with module-level mutable state is called from several threads without a lock
javascript: worker or async code shares a function that keeps state in module variables across await points
rust: libc non-reentrant functions such as strtok or localtime called through FFI from several threads

c: reentrant variants such as strtok_r, localtime_r or gmtime_r are used
calls are serialised by a lock, or the program is single-threaded
cpp: only the static's initialisation is shared, which C++11 makes thread-safe, and later access is read-only or under a std::mutex
python: the shared state is protected by a lock or is per-thread
javascript: the code runs on a single thread and does no await between reading and updating the shared state
rust: only safe Rust APIs are used, with shared state behind Mutex or atomics

distinguish_from.CWE-479: the call is made from a signal handler

CWE-667.name: Improper Locking
CWE-667.question: Does this function acquire or release a lock incorrectly, such as missing a release on some path, releasing twice, or taking locks in an inconsistent order?

any: a lock is acquired and an early return, error branch or exception leaves without releasing it
a lock is released twice, or released on a path where it was never acquired
two or more locks are taken in an order that differs from other code in the function
shared data is touched after the lock protecting it has been released
locking uses a scope-based guard, with statement or finally block so release happens on every path
rust: locks are held through MutexGuard values released on drop
cpp: std::lock_guard, unique_lock or scoped_lock manage the lock
javascript: the code runs single-threaded with no explicit lock objects

distinguish_from.CWE-833: the locking order creates a circular wait
distinguish_from.CWE-764: the same lock is acquired more times than intended
distinguish_from.CWE-765: the same lock is released more times than intended

CWE-689.name: Permission Race Condition During Resource Copy
CWE-689.question: Does this function copy or create a file or resource and set its restrictive permissions only after the content has been written?

c: a file is created with open or fopen using default or broad permissions, filled, and only then chmod-ed or chown-ed
a directory tree is copied and permissions are applied in a final pass after all content is written
cpp: std::ofstream writes the content and std::filesystem::permissions restricts the file only afterwards

c: the file is created with restrictive mode bits in the open call, or umask is tightened first
the copy is made in a private directory and moved into place after permissions are set
the content is not sensitive and default permissions are intended

distinguish_from.CWE-363: a file is checked and then used, and could be swapped for a link

CWE-764.name: Multiple Locks of a Critical Resource
CWE-764.question: Can this function lock the same lock more times than intended, for example locking a non-recursive mutex it already holds?

any: a lock is acquired and, on some path, acquired again before being released
the function holds a lock and calls a helper that takes the same lock
a lock is acquired inside a loop with the release outside it
c: pthread_mutex_lock called twice on a default (non-recursive) mutex on one path
cpp: a std::lock_guard or m.lock() on a std::mutex the function already holds, such as a member that locks calling another member that locks the same mutex
python: a threading.Lock (not RLock) is acquired while already held by the same thread
rust: lock() is called on a Mutex while a guard from the same Mutex is still alive

any: each acquire is matched by a release before the next acquire on every path
the lock is explicitly recursive and each acquire has a matching release
cpp: the mutex is a std::recursive_mutex with balanced locking, or each scope takes one std::scoped_lock and calls only unlocked helpers
javascript: the code uses no explicit lock objects, as ordinary single-threaded JS has none

distinguish_from.CWE-833: two or more different locks are waited on in a cycle
distinguish_from.CWE-765: the lock is released too many times

CWE-765.name: Multiple Unlocks of a Critical Resource
CWE-765.question: Can this function unlock the same lock more times than it locked it on some path?

any: a lock is released in an error branch and again in common cleanup on the same path
a release appears in a loop or in several branches that can all run after one acquire
c: pthread_mutex_unlock or a semaphore post is called twice for one lock
cpp: m.unlock() called manually while a std::lock_guard or std::unique_lock still owns m, so the guard releases it a second time at scope exit
python: release() is called both in a branch and in finally after a single acquire()

any: each acquire has exactly one release on every path
locking uses a scope-based guard or with statement that releases once
cpp: the lock is held by std::lock_guard or std::scoped_lock with no manual unlock, or owns_lock() is checked before a std::unique_lock is unlocked
javascript: the code uses no explicit lock objects, as ordinary single-threaded JS has none
rust: the lock is released only by dropping its guard, which cannot happen twice

distinguish_from.CWE-832: the unlock happens on a lock never acquired at all
distinguish_from.CWE-764: the lock is acquired too many times

CWE-820.name: Missing Synchronization
CWE-820.question: Does this function read or modify state shared with other threads, workers or concurrent tasks without any lock, atomic or other synchronisation at all?

any: a global, static, class-level or captured variable is updated by code that the function itself runs on several threads, tasks or callbacks, and no lock or atomic is used anywhere around it
the function starts threads or workers that all write the same object or counter with plain reads and writes
c: a static or global is read-modify-written (count++, list insert) in a thread routine or signal handler with no mutex, atomic or volatile sig_atomic_t
cpp: a std::thread, std::async or std::jthread lambda captures by reference and writes a shared counter or container with no std::mutex or std::atomic
javascript: a SharedArrayBuffer is read and written by workers with plain indexing instead of Atomics
module-level state is read before an await and written back after it with no guard against interleaved calls
python: a module-level or instance attribute is modified from threading.Thread or executor targets with no Lock
rust: a static mut, UnsafeCell or raw pointer is accessed from spawned threads inside unsafe with no Mutex or atomic

any: every access to the shared state is inside a lock, atomic operation or other synchronisation primitive
the state is local to the function or owned by a single thread or task
the function is not run concurrently, and nothing in it starts threads, workers or concurrent tasks
cpp: the shared value is a std::atomic, or every access holds a std::lock_guard on the same mutex
rust: the sharing goes through safe Rust types such as Arc<Mutex>, RwLock, atomics or channels, which the compiler checks

distinguish_from.CWE-821: a lock or other synchronisation is used but is the wrong kind, covers too little, or is applied inconsistently
distinguish_from.CWE-362: the defect is a check-then-act window between two steps rather than a total absence of synchronisation
distinguish_from.CWE-1096: the unsynchronised code is specifically the lazy creation of a singleton instance

CWE-821.name: Incorrect Synchronization
CWE-821.question: Does this function synchronise access to shared state, but in a way that is wrong or incomplete, such as the wrong lock, too narrow a section or only some accesses guarded?

any: the same shared variable is accessed under a lock on one path and without it on another path in this function
the lock is released between reading shared state and writing a result based on it, so the update is not atomic as a whole
different accesses to one shared resource use different locks, or each call creates a fresh lock object
c: a volatile qualifier is relied on as if it made a read-modify-write atomic
cpp: a std::atomic updated as x.store(x.load() + 1) or x = x + 1, or a std::lock_guard scoped in an inner block that closes before the dependent write
python: threading.Lock() is created inside the function on every call, so callers never share it
rust: a Mutex guard is dropped and the lock re-acquired between a read and a dependent write inside unsafe or with shared raw pointers

any: every access to the shared state is covered by the same lock held for the whole read-modify-write sequence
the shared state is accessed only through atomic operations that do the full update in one step
there is no shared state; everything is local or owned by one thread
cpp: fetch_add, compare_exchange or one std::lock_guard spanning the whole read-modify-write is used
rust: sharing uses safe Rust types and the guard spans the whole update

distinguish_from.CWE-820: no synchronisation is attempted at all
distinguish_from.CWE-667: the defect is in acquiring or releasing the lock itself, such as an unlock that is skipped or a lock taken twice
distinguish_from.CWE-362: the defect is a race window between a check and the dependent action with no lock involved

CWE-828.name: Signal Handler with Functionality that is not Asynchronous-Safe
CWE-828.question: Does this signal handler do work that is not async-signal-safe, such as allocating memory, taking locks, doing buffered I/O or changing shared structures?

any: a signal handler updates linked lists, counters or other shared structures that normal code also updates
c: a handler calls malloc, free, printf, syslog, fopen or a mutex function
cpp: a signal handler uses std::cout, std::string, new, std::mutex, a non-lock-free std::atomic or throws an exception
python: a signal handler does long work, takes a lock that the main code may hold, or logs through handlers that lock
javascript: a process.on signal handler synchronously changes state that an in-progress operation relies on
rust: a raw libc signal handler allocates, locks a Mutex or uses println!

any: the handler only sets an atomic or volatile sig_atomic_t flag, or writes to a self-pipe
c: the handler calls only async-signal-safe functions such as write or _exit
cpp: the handler only stores to a lock-free std::atomic or a volatile std::sig_atomic_t
rust: signals are handled through signal-hook flag or iterator helpers rather than custom raw handlers

distinguish_from.CWE-479: the unsafe call is to a specific non-reentrant library function
distinguish_from.CWE-432: the issue is not masking other signals that share state

CWE-831.name: Signal Handler Function Associated with Multiple Signals
CWE-831.question: Does this function register one handler for several different signals, where that handler touches shared state or has side effects?

any: the same handler function is installed for two or more signals, and it modifies global data, frees resources or calls non-reentrant code
c: signal or sigaction is called for SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGHUP or others all naming one handler that changes globals
python: signal.signal is called for several signals with the same function, which changes module-level state
javascript: process.on is called for several signal names with one callback that mutates shared state or starts cleanup twice
rust: signal-hook or libc registration of one handler for multiple signals that writes static data

any: the shared handler only sets an atomic flag or records the signal number atomically
each signal has its own handler, or the shared handler uses only local data
c: the handler's sa_mask blocks the other signals it handles while it runs

distinguish_from.CWE-432: different handlers share state without masking each other
distinguish_from.CWE-828: the handler's problem is calling unsafe code regardless of how many signals it serves

CWE-832.name: Unlock of a Resource that is not Locked
CWE-832.question: Can this function release a lock that it has not acquired on that path?

any: the acquire is conditional or can fail, but the release in shared cleanup runs regardless
a function unlocks a lock that is only acquired in some callers, with no check
c: pthread_mutex_trylock fails or is skipped, yet pthread_mutex_unlock is called
cpp: m.unlock() on a std::mutex in cleanup reached when try_lock() returned false or before lock() ran
a std::unique_lock made with std::defer_lock or std::try_to_lock is unlocked without checking owns_lock()
python: acquire(blocking=False) returns False, yet release() is called

any: the release is only reached on paths where the acquire succeeded
a scope-based guard or with statement manages the lock
cpp: a std::unique_lock or std::lock_guard releases at scope exit only what it owns
javascript: the code uses no explicit lock objects, as ordinary single-threaded JS has none
rust: the lock is released only by dropping the guard returned from a successful lock

distinguish_from.CWE-765: the lock was acquired once but is released more than once

CWE-833.name: Deadlock
CWE-833.question: Can this function deadlock, for example by taking two locks in an order that other code reverses, or by waiting for something while holding the lock it needs?

any: two locks are acquired in nested fashion, and the function also shows or calls code acquiring them in the opposite order
a thread joins or waits for another thread or task while holding a lock that the other needs
a blocking call (queue put, channel send, future result) is made while holding a lock the consumer must take
javascript: an async function awaits a promise that can only resolve after the same async mutex or semaphore is released

any: only one lock is held at a time
multiple locks are always taken in one fixed order, or together with a deadlock-avoiding helper
no blocking wait is made while a lock is held
cpp: std::scoped_lock or std::lock acquires several mutexes together

distinguish_from.CWE-764: a single lock is re-acquired by the same thread

CWE-1058.name: Invokable Control Element in Multi-Thread Context with non-Final Static Storable or Member Element
CWE-1058.question: Does this function, which may run on several threads, write to a mutable static, class-level or shared member field rather than to local or per-call state?

any: the function assigns to or mutates a static variable, class attribute or field of a shared object (such as a handler, servlet-like controller or singleton) that is not constant, without a lock
c: a function-scope static or file-scope global that is not const is written in code reachable from multiple threads
cpp: a static data member or member of a shared object is modified by a method that request or worker threads call
javascript: a worker or request handler mutates module-level or class static state that concurrent requests share
typescript: an instance field of a NestJS @Injectable() provider, a singleton by default, is written with per-request data
python: a method of a shared object called from threads assigns to a class attribute or self attribute used as scratch storage
rust: a static mut is written inside unsafe from code that threads can reach

any: the static or member is const, final or never written after initialisation
writes are protected by a lock or use atomics
the state written is local, thread-local or per-request
typescript: the provider is declared with scope: Scope.REQUEST, or per-request data stays in local variables or the request object
rust: only safe Rust is used, so shared statics can be mutated only through Mutex, atomics or other Sync types

distinguish_from.CWE-820: the code shows shared state used concurrently without synchronisation but not specifically a static or member element
distinguish_from.CWE-488: the consequence is one user's or session's data being handed to another

CWE-1088.name: Synchronous Access of Remote Resource without Timeout
CWE-1088.question: Does this function make a blocking call to a remote service, socket or database without a timeout, or with an infinite timeout?

any: a blocking network, HTTP, RPC or database call is made with no timeout argument and no timeout set on the client, connection or socket beforehand
a timeout is explicitly set to zero, None, -1 or infinite where that means wait forever
c: connect, recv, read or SSL_read on a blocking socket with no SO_RCVTIMEO, poll or select deadline
curl_easy_perform with no CURLOPT_TIMEOUT or CURLOPT_CONNECTTIMEOUT set
cpp: a synchronous Boost.Asio connect, read or read_until on a socket with no deadline timer or socket timeout option set
javascript: a synchronous child_process.execSync or spawnSync to a remote command with no timeout option, or a request client configured with timeout 0
python: requests.get or post, urllib.request.urlopen, socket.recv or a DB connect is called without a timeout argument
rust: a blocking TcpStream read or ureq/reqwest blocking call with no read or connect timeout configured

any: a finite timeout or deadline is passed to the call or set on the client or socket before it
the call is to a local in-process function or local file, not a remote resource
the call is asynchronous and the function wraps it in a timeout or cancellation
cpp: asynchronous Asio operations are paired with a steady_timer that cancels them when the deadline passes
javascript: the call uses fetch or another promise-based API in non-blocking code with an AbortSignal timeout

distinguish_from.CWE-1322: the issue is a blocking call made inside an event loop or other non-blocking context regardless of any timeout
distinguish_from.CWE-400: the wider concern is resource exhaustion from many waiting calls rather than one call lacking a timeout

CWE-1096.name: Singleton Class Instance Creation without Proper Locking or Synchronization
CWE-1096.question: Does this function lazily create a singleton or one-time shared instance in a way that two concurrent callers could both create it?

any: the function tests whether a shared instance exists and creates and stores it if not, with no lock, once-guard or atomic compare-and-set around the test and the store
c: a static pointer is checked for NULL and then malloc'd or constructed, without pthread_once, call_once or a mutex
javascript: a cached instance or promise is created after an await that sits between the existence check and the assignment, so overlapping calls each create one
python: a class attribute or module global such as _instance is checked and assigned in code called from threads without a Lock
rust: a static mut Option is checked and assigned inside unsafe instead of using OnceLock, LazyLock or Once

any: creation is protected by a lock held across both the check and the assignment, or by a once primitive
the instance is created eagerly at start-up before any concurrency begins
cpp: the instance is a function-local static, which C++11 initialises thread-safely
javascript: the check and assignment happen synchronously with no await between them, so the single-threaded event loop cannot interleave callers
rust: OnceLock, LazyLock, OnceCell or lazy_static is used, which guarantee one initialisation

distinguish_from.CWE-543: the C++ code is a classic getInstance singleton, which is the more precise entry
distinguish_from.CWE-609: a lock exists but the unsynchronised first check of double-checked locking is the flaw

CWE-1232.name: Improper Lock Behavior After Power State Transition
CWE-1232.question: Does this firmware function, on resume from sleep or another power state change, restore protected configuration without setting the lock bits again?

any: a resume, wake or power-up handler restores configuration registers but does not set the lock bit or write-protect flag
the lock bit is written only in cold-boot code, while the warm-resume path skips it
the resume path sets the same lock bits as the cold-boot path after restoring configuration
the function is not firmware handling power state transitions
python: ordinary Python application code does not program hardware lock registers
javascript: ordinary JavaScript code does not program hardware lock registers

distinguish_from.CWE-1234: the lock is bypassed because a debug or test mode is active

CWE-1234.name: Hardware Internal or Debug Modes Allow Override of Locks
CWE-1234.question: Does this firmware or low-level function let a debug, test or manufacturing mode skip or override configuration lock protection?

any: a write to a locked register or protected setting is allowed when a debug, test or JTAG flag is set
the lock bit is not set, or is cleared, when a debug mode is detected at start-up
lock enforcement does not depend on any debug or test mode flag
entering debug mode clears secrets or blocks access to protected settings
the function is not firmware handling hardware locks
python: ordinary Python application code does not program hardware lock registers
javascript: ordinary JavaScript code does not program hardware lock registers

distinguish_from.CWE-1232: the lock is lost after a power state change rather than through a debug mode

CWE-1264.name: Hardware Logic with Insecure De-Synchronization between Control and Data Channels
CWE-1264.reason: Concerns hardware logic forwarding data on separate bus or datapath channels, not software function code.

CWE-1265.name: Unintended Reentrant Invocation of Non-reentrant Code Via Nested Calls
CWE-1265.question: Can this non-reentrant function call out, through a callback, hook, signal, event or nested call, into code that may re-enter it while its state is half-updated?

any: the function invokes a caller-supplied callback, listener, virtual method or user hook while shared or object state is partly modified and no reentrancy guard is set
the function updates a static buffer or global and, before finishing, calls something that can call back into the same function
c: a signal handler, interrupt routine or callback can call a function that uses static buffers, malloc or stdio while it is running
cpp: a loop over a std::vector of listeners calls each one while a callback can add or remove entries in that same vector
javascript: an event is emitted or a callback invoked inside a loop over internal state that the listener can modify by calling back in
python: __del__, a callback or a dunder method called mid-update can re-enter the method that is mutating the object
rust: a callback is invoked while a RefCell borrow_mut is held, so re-entry would panic, or unsafe code mutates state that the callback can reach

any: all state changes are complete before any external code is called
a reentrancy flag, lock or depth counter prevents nested invocation
the function calls no callbacks, hooks or user-supplied code

distinguish_from.CWE-663: a known non-reentrant library function such as strtok or localtime is called from concurrent threads
distinguish_from.CWE-820: the problem is concurrent threads accessing shared state, not a nested call on the same thread
